title: PREVAIL-Study: effects of PREssure vs Volume controlled ventilAtion on preterm Infants' Lung volumes
summary:
Some premature infants require invasive mechanical ventilation using a breathing tube. Volume-controlled and pressure-controlled ventilation are the primary methods used. Volume-controlled ventilation is currently considered the gentler option for the lungs. Nevertheless, the lungs of some preterm infants cannot always be ventilated evenly and optimally using this method. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood.
To better understand this, lung ventilation in preterm infants is being studied using electrical impedance tomography (EIT), which allows for real-time visualization of air distribution within the lungs. Using this measurement method, we aim to investigate how lung ventilation differs in these infants under volume-controlled and pressure-controlled ventilation. In the long term, the results should help to further improve ventilation for premature infants and adapt it more precisely to the needs of each individual child. Ventilation that is as protective as possible can help reduce the risk of ventilator-induced chronic lung diseases.
conditions: Disorders related to short gestation and low birth weight, not elsewhere classified

interventions.name: The children are randomized into two intervention arms using a crossover design. The ventilation mode—either volume-controlled (VCV) or pressure-controlled (PCV)—is administered continuously for 60 minutes each in a randomized order. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Age > 48 hours postnatal
- Indication for conventional, invasive ventilation (pressure- or volume-controlled)
Exclusion criteria:
- Endotracheal tube leakage >30%
- Children on invasive ventilation with pneumothorax
- Congenital pulmonary malformations or genetic syndromes with pulmonary impairment
